root_cause: When the #more button removes itself while focused, the focus trap's state.mostRecentlyFocusedNode retains a reference to the detached element. The checkFocusIn handler attempts to restore focus via tryFocus(state.mostRecentlyFocusedNode), but tryFocus does not verify the node is still in the document, causing node.focus() to fail silently. Additionally, the trap's internal tabbable node cache (state.tabbableGroups) becomes stale after DOM mutations, so getInitialFocusNode() may return an outdated reference.
repair_strategy: Harden tryFocus to reject nodes no longer contained in the document (using doc.contains(node)) and fall back to getInitialFocusNode(). Modify checkFocusIn to refresh the trap's tabbable node cache via updateTabbableNodes() before requesting the initial focus node when focus escapes, ensuring a live reference to the first focusable element (#close).
expected_accessibility_effect: After clicking the #more button (which removes itself), focus will remain trapped inside the dialog on the #close button (the first tabbable element), ensuring keyboard users can continue to navigate the dialog without accidentally leaving it. The Escape key will still close the dialog and return focus to the #open button.
functional_risks: The updateTabbableNodes call on every focus escape adds minimal overhead but runs synchronously.
If the first container has no tabbable nodes (unlikely, as the trap requires at least one), the fallback may still fail.
The tryFocus hardening adds a safety net for any other code paths that might pass a detached node.
verification_requirements: After clicking the #more button, pressing Tab should move focus to the #close button (not to the body).
The dialog should retain focus within after the #more button is removed (verified by #results:focus-within).
The Escape key should still close the dialog and return focus to the #open button.
The initial focus when opening the dialog should remain on the #close button.
